40418625.what_the_study_did: The study developed an integrated AI-PBPK platform to estimate drug in vivo fate and tissue distribution based on molecular structures.
40418625.what_it_found: The AI-PBPK platform showed robust results, with most AUC predictions falling within two and threefold error ranges when validated against human PK data.

key_quotes.quote: The AI models were trained to predict eight types of key properties (solubility, pKa values, crystal density, intrinsic dissolution rate, apparent permeability, protein unbound fraction, plasma clearance, and tissue partition coefficients for 15 organs), from which the PBPK model forecasted PK curves without further training.
The AI-PBPK approach was validated against human PK data of 71 intravenous and 606 oral administrations collected from the PK-DB database.
The results were robust, with most of the AUC predictions falling within two and threefold error ranges.
The AI-PBPK model also accurately predicted drug organ selectivity, and for drugs exhibiting high plasma clearance, predictions were optimized through an inter-species extrapolation approach.
The modeling system can guide candidate selection, advancing more drugs with favorable PK profiles into clinical trials, thereby significantly enhancing the efficiency of drug development.

38642821.what_the_study_did: This study investigated sex, age, and species differences of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) using physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models in rats and humans.
38642821.what_it_found: Both flow-limited and permeability-limited PBPK models successfully captured sex differences in rats, but only the flow-limited model with male rats and the permeability-limited model with both male and female rats provided comparable predictions to a human clinical study.

key_quotes.quote: Our results showed that both models successfully captured sex differences in rats, while only the flow-limited model with male rats and the permeability-limited model with both male and female rats provided comparable predictions in the human clinical study.
More than the flow-limited model, the permeability-limited model effectively explained sex differences in rats and species differences through IVIVE.
Additionally, the ontogeny-based mechanistic description of PFOA disposition enabled the interpretation of age- and sex-dependent pharmacokinetics.
Although the flow-limited PBPK model lacked mechanistic interpretability compared to the permeability-limited model, it demonstrated reliable human prediction through simple allometric scaling.
In conclusion, the permeability PBPK model could interpret age, sex, and species differences and it could improve the accuracy of human prediction.

32735877.what_the_study_did: The study explored how to strategically combine toxicological tests to maximize their predictive power, using the prediction of cardiac arrhythmia torsade de pointes as an example.
32735877.what_it_found: Tests can be strategically combined to reach a desired level of predictive power, which is generally more easily achieved for negative predictive power when the toxicity prevalence is low.

key_quotes.quote: Overall, the analysis demonstrates that tests can be strategically combined to reach a desired level of predictive power.
This is generally more easily achieved for negative predictive power given a low prevalence of the toxicity under scrutiny.
For this work, we used a base prevalence of 10% for a substance to carry a tordsadogenic liability.
Given uncertainty around a test's discriminatory power, a probabilistic rather than deterministic approach was recommended.
The proposed approach is easily implemented deterministically since values of the discriminatory power of the tests are readily and publicly available.
This general approach could form a basis for testing and decision-making that can be communicated and discussed in a consistent manner between scientists as well as between sponsors and regulators.

32152206.what_the_study_did: The study presents a framework called PAMERAH for predicting the therapeutic efficacy of a glucose-responsive insulin (GRI) candidate based on its mechanism of action, kinetics, and dosage, built upon a previous human model.
32152206.what_it_found: The PAMERAH framework is accurate when checked against experimental data and literature, and simulated glucose clamp results quantitatively agree with recent GRI publications.

key_quotes.quote: Results from simulated glucose clamps also agree quantitatively with recent GRI publications.

We demonstrate that the model can be used to explore the vast number of permutations constituting the GRI parameter space and thereby identify the optimal design ranges that yield desired performance.
PAMERAH more importantly can facilitate GRI's clinical translation by connecting each candidate's efficacies in rats, mice, and humans.
The resultant mapping helps to find GRIs that appear promising in rodents but underperform in humans (i.e., false positives).
Conversely, it also allows for the discovery of optimal human GRI dynamics not captured by experiments on a rodent population (false negatives).

key_quotes.quote: The most comprehensive survey of clinical success rates across the drug industry to date shows productivity may be even lower than previous estimates.
We found that approximately one in ten (10.4%, n = 5,820) of all indication development paths in phase 1 were approved by FDA (Fig. 1 and Table 4).

Achieving FDA approval for only one-in-ten drug indications that enter the clinic is a concerning statistic for drug developers, regulators, investors and patients.

24489990.what_the_study_did: This review critically evaluates pre-clinical animal models and their role in translation to clinical practice for cancer patients, discussing limitations and alternative strategies.
24489990.what_it_found: The average rate of successful translation from animal models to clinical cancer trials is less than 8%, with many failures attributed to differences in physiology and molecular targets between species.

key_quotes.quote: However, the average rate of successful translation from animal models to clinical cancer trials is less than 8%.
Animal models are limited in their ability to mimic the extremely complex process of human carcinogenesis, physiology and progression.
Indeed, animal studies seem to overestimate by about 30% the likelihood that a treatment will be effective because negative results are often unpublished [9].
Crucial genetic, molecular, immunologic and cellular differences between humans and mice prevent animal models from serving as effective means to seek for a cancer cure [13].
The failure to translate from animals to humans is likely due in part to poor methodology and failure of the models to accurately mimic the human disease condition.
The vast majority of agents that are found to be successful in animal models do not pan out in human trials.

It was acknowledged from the outset that some of the data might not hold up, because papers were deliberately selected that described something completely new, such as fresh approaches to targeting cancers or alternative clinical uses for existing therapeutics. Nevertheless, scientific findings were confirmed in only 6 (11%) cases.

22460880.what_the_study_did: The authors reviewed the reproducibility of landmark preclinical cancer research findings and the ability of industry to validate these findings for drug development.
22460880.what_it_found: A significant proportion of landmark preclinical cancer research findings were not reproducible, and only about 25% of published preclinical studies could be validated for drug development.

key_quotes.quote: Many landmark findings in preclinical oncology research are not reproducible, in part because of inadequate cell lines and animal models.
Historically, our ability to translate cancer research to clinical success has been remarkably low.
Fifty-three papers were deemed ‘landmark’ studies... Nevertheless, scientific findings were confirmed in only 6 (11%) cases.
A team at Bayer HealthCare in Germany last year reported4 that only about 25% of published preclinical studies could be validated to the point at which projects could continue.

The limitations of preclinical tools such as inadequate cancer-cell-line and mouse models make it difficult for even the best scientists working in optimal conditions to make a discovery that will ultimately have an impact in the clinic.
The inability of industry and clinical trials to validate results from the majority of publications on potential therapeutic targets suggests a general, systemic problem.

25092317.what_the_study_did: The study reevaluated gene expression datasets from a previous study that claimed mouse models poorly mimic human inflammatory diseases, using different statistical methods.
25092317.what_it_found: Contrary to the previous findings, the gene expression patterns in mouse models showed significant correlations with human conditions, suggesting their utility as animal models.

key_quotes.quote: Contrary to the previous findings, the gene expression levels in the mouse models showed extraordinarily significant correlations with those of the human conditions (Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient: 0.43–0.68; genes changed in the same direction: 77– 93%; P = 6.5 × 10−11 to 1.2 × 10−35).

These findings demonstrate that gene expression patterns in mouse models closely recapitulate those in human inflammatory conditions and strongly argue for the utility of mice as animal models of human disorders.

Murine models were highly significantly correlated with human conditions with Spearman’s correlation coefficient (ρ = 0.43–0.68; P < 0.0001 for every comparison between human conditions and mouse models).
The correlations between different mouse models were also significant (ρ = 0.47–0.57; P < 0.0001 for every comparison between a pair of mouse models).

Nonparametric ranking analysis by NextBio rejected, with extraordinarily high confidence, the hypothesis that mouse models show only coincidental overlap of the directionality of gene changes with those in human burn conditions [Fig. 2; overlap P value = 3.9 × 10−34, 6.3 × 10−13, 1.2 × 10−35, 6.5 × 10−11, and 3.4 × 10−35 for mouse models of burn, trauma, sepsis (GSE19668), sepsis (GSE26472), and infection, respectively], demonstrating that the directionality of the changes in mouse models was highly similar to that in human burn conditions.

Contrary to the conclusion of Seok et al., there were significant correlations and similarities of the direction in the gene expression changes between human burn conditions and mouse models (Fig. 3; human: fold change >2.0; mouse model: fold change >1.2; R = 0.26–0.51; P < 0.0001 for all comparisons; percentage: 48.1–86.2).

21892149.what_the_study_did: The study analyzed 67 in-house drug target identification and validation projects to assess the reproducibility of published data.
21892149.what_it_found: In approximately 20-25% of projects, published data completely aligned with in-house findings, while inconsistencies led to project termination in most cases.

key_quotes.quote: This analysis revealed that only in ~20–25% of the projects were the relevant published data completely in line with our inhouse findings (FIG. 1c).

In almost two-thirds of the projects, there were inconsistencies between published data and in-house data that either considerably prolonged the duration of the target validation process or, in most cases, resulted in termination of the projects because the evidence that was generated for the therapeutic hypothesis was insufficient to justify further investments into these projects.

Rather, either the results were reproducible and showed transferability in other models, or even a 1:1 reproduction of published experimental procedures revealed inconsistencies between published and in-house data (FIG. 1d).
Surprisingly, even publications in prestigious journals or from several independent groups did not ensure reproducibility.

An unspoken rule among early-stage venture capital firms that “at least 50% of published studies, even those in top-tier academic journals, can’t be repeated with the same conclusions by an industrial lab” has been recently reported (see Further information) and discussed4.

Our observations indicate that literature data on potential drug targets should be viewed with caution, and underline the importance of confirmatory validation studies for pharmaceutical companies and academia before larger investments are made in assay development, high-throughput screening campaigns, lead optimization and animal testing.

28893587.what_the_study_did: The study created and analyzed a nonclinical to clinical translational database of 182 molecules to determine how safety assessments in animal models translate to First-In-Human clinical risk.
28893587.what_it_found: The study found that while nonclinical studies have value in predicting certain toxicities, the negative predictive value (NPV) is the strongest predictive performance measure, indicating that an absence of toxicity in animal studies strongly predicts a similar outcome in the clinic.

key_quotes.quote: Sensitivity was 48% with a 43% positive predictive value (PPV).
Speciﬁcity was 84% with an 86% negative predictive value (NPV).
The nonhuman primate had the strongest performance in predicting adverse eﬀects, especially for gastrointestinal and nervous system categories.

While nonclinical studies can demonstrate great value in the PPV for certain species and organ categories, the NPV was the stronger predictive performance measure across test species and target organs indicating that an absence of toxicity in animal studies strongly predicts a similar outcome in the clinic.
The value of the standard two-species testing paradigm goes beyond simply expanding the breadth of target organs identiﬁed.
The NPV is the stronger predictive performance measure that was derived from our database, signifying that a lack of toxicity in animal studies strongly predicts safety in phase I.

20613859.what_the_study_did: The study developed and described the ARRIVE guidelines for reporting animal research to improve the quality and transparency of publications.
20613859.what_it_found: A review of published animal research found significant omissions in reporting, with only 59% of articles stating the hypothesis or objective and animal characteristics, and many failing to report randomisation, blinding, or statistical methods.

key_quotes.quote: The largest and most comprehensive review of published animal research undertaken to date, as far as we are aware, has highlighted serious omissions in the way research using animals is reported [5].

only 59% of the 271 randomly chosen articles assessed stated the hypothesis or objective of the study, and the number and characteristics of the animals used (i.e., species/strain, sex, and age/weight).
Most of the papers surveyed did not report using randomisation (87%) or blinding (86%) to reduce bias in animal selection and outcome assessment.
Only 70% of the publications that used statistical methods fully described them and presented the results with a measure of precision or variability [5].
4% of the 271 journal articles assessed did not report the number of animals used anywhere in the methods or the results sections [5].

Improved reporting of these and other details will maximise the availability and utility of the information gained from every animal and every experiment, preventing unnecessary animal use in the future.

34874005.what_the_study_did: The study aimed to assess the replicability of preclinical cancer biology research by repeating experiments from high-impact papers.
34874005.what_it_found: Replications generally provided weaker evidence than the original papers, with lower effect sizes and varying success rates depending on the criterion used.

key_quotes.quote: Their success rates (25% for the Bayer report, and 11% for the Amgen report) provided disquieting initial evidence that preclinical research may be much less replicable than recognized.
These challenges meant that we only completed 50 of the 193 experiments (26%) we planned to repeat.

For original positive effects, 42 of the 97 (43%) replication effects were statistically significant and in the same direction as the original effect; 48 (49%) were null results; and 7 (7%) were statistically significant in the opposite direction.
We found that 17 of the 97 (18%) original positive effect sizes were in the 95% confidence interval of the replication effect size, as were 11 of the 15 (73%) original null effect sizes.

For the 97 effects that were positive in the original experiments, we find that just 13 were successful on all three criteria, 18 were successful on two, 26 were successful on one, and 40 failed to replicate on all three criteria.
Animal experiments with positive effects were less likely to replicate than non-animal experiments with positive effects on every replication criterion.

31827124.what_the_study_did: The study developed a probabilistic framework to estimate the probability of drug development success based on target identification methods, comparing traditional preclinical studies with genomic approaches like GWAS.
31827124.what_it_found: A genomic approach to target identification significantly increases the probability of drug development success compared to traditional preclinical methods, primarily by reducing the false discovery rate and improving the accuracy of target selection.

key_quotes.quote: The poor predictive ability of preclinical studies for human efficacy (an aspect of the so-called ‘reproducibility crisis’ in laboratory science) can be attributed in part to correctable flaws in experimental design including infrequent use of randomisation and blinding 22 – 25 . However, errors of statistical inference leading to a high false discovery ( FDR ) rate may be equally important.

GWAS overcome many of the design flaws inherent in standard preclinical testing in isolated cells, tissues and animal models. They are an experiment in the correct organism (the human); have the lowest false discovery rate in any field of biomedicine (Supplementary Note 3 ); provide the systematic, concurrent interrogation of every potential drug target on the condition of interest (rather than a few targets selected from a larger pool); and exploit the unique attributes of genetic variation (fixed and allocated at random), which mimics the design of the pivotal experiment in drug development, the RCT 41 – 44 .

In striking contrast, with the same sample space but a genomic approach to target identification, where (1 − β ) = 0.8, α = 5 × 10 −8 and all 20,000 targets encoded by the genome are, by definition, interrogated simultaneously, TDR pc = 0.999, and FDR pc = 0.001.

The fundamental problem in contemporary drug development has been the unreliability of target identification leading to low development success rates, inefficiency and escalating cost to healthcare users. Genomics now provides a tool to address the problem directly by accurate identification of proteins that both play a controlling role in a disease and which are amenable to targeting by drugs.

By improving the efficiency and reliability of target identification, GWAS and similar genetic study designs offer the potential to overturn the currently poor odds of success currently beleaguering drug development.
The performance of genomic studies for target identification, based on these values of α and 1 − β , is little affected by 100-fold differences in C ¯ and γ pc (Table 4 ).

21350617.what_the_study_did: The study reviewed the reporting quality of bioscience research, particularly animal research, and developed the ARRIVE guidelines to improve it.
21350617.what_it_found: A significant proportion of published animal research articles lack essential details regarding study design, methods, and results, hindering their utility and reproducibility.

key_quotes.quote: The survey, commissioned by the National Centre for the Replacement, Refinement and Reduction of Animals in Research (NC3Rs), a UK Government-sponsored scientific organisation, found that only 59% of the 271 randomly chosen articles assessed stated the hypothesis or objective of the study and the number and characteristics of the animals used (i.e., species/strain, sex and age/weight).
Most of the papers surveyed did not report using randomisation (87%) or blinding (86%) to reduce bias in animal selection and outcome assessment.
Only 70% of the publications that used statistical methods fully described them and presented the results with a measure of precision or variability.
Our review found that 4% of the 271 journal articles assessed did not report the number of animals used anywhere in the methods or the results sections.
Convincing evidence is emerging that CONSORT improves the quality and transparency of reports of clinical trials.

The ARRIVE guidelines consist of a checklist of 20 items describing the minimum information that all scientific publications reporting research using animals should include, such as the number and specific characteristics of animals used (including species, strain, sex and genetic background); details of housing and husbandry; and the experimental, statistical and analytical methods (including details of methods used to reduce bias such as randomisation and blinding).

26863229.what_the_study_did: The study developed a quantitative decision model to analyze factors influencing R&D decisions and explored these factors through quantitative analyses.
26863229.what_it_found: The study found that predictive validity (PV) has a powerful effect on R&D decision quality and productivity, and that improvements in PV can offset large changes in brute-force efficiency.

key_quotes.quote: Changes in the PV of decision variables that many people working in drug discovery would regard as small and/or unknowable (i.e., a 0.1 absolute change in correlation coefficient versus clinical outcome) can offset large (e.g., 10 fold or greater) changes in brute-force efficiency.
The second important result is the interaction between y t and ρ Y , R on PPV (see how the orientation of the contours changes in Fig 4 ).
Increasing throughput by several orders of magnitude has a minimal positive effect on PPV when ρ Y , R is very low.
Modest gains in ρ Y , R can have very large positive effect on PPV when throughput is high.
In practical terms, there is little point in investing to increase the throughput of a poor PM or the stringency of the classifier based on that PM.
It may often make sense to seek out and add PMs that have face validity versus R but which yield decision variables that have a low correlation with other decision variables.

28328898.what_the_study_did: The study proposes a framework for improving the harm-benefit analysis of animal research by systematically assessing the scientific validity of studies, in addition to the 3Rs (Replacement, Reduction, Refinement).
28328898.what_it_found: The study found that multi-laboratory designs can significantly increase the reproducibility of research findings compared to single-laboratory studies, and that less than 50% of single-laboratory studies produce an accurate estimate of the true effect size.

key_quotes.quote: Unless a study produces results that are scientifically valid and reproducible, the animals may be wasted for inconclusive research, no matter how little harm is inflicted on them1.
Over the past decade, evidence has accumulated indicating that scientific validity and reproducibility are alarmingly poor throughout biomedical research1,5.
Based on systematic reviews and s­ imulations, Ioannidis concluded that “for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true”6.

whereas less than 50% of single-laboratory studies produced an accurate estimate of the “true” effect size (reduction of infarct volume by 48%, as assessed by meta-analysis), simulations showed that multilaboratory studies based on as few as three laboratories can increase reproducibility from less than 50% to over 80%, without increasing false negative rate or a need for larger sample sizes30.
At present, ethical review does not include a systematic assessment of scientific validity in the course of HBA.

35167625.what_the_study_did: This systematic review and meta-analysis analyzed IRAK3 expression and its effects on inflammatory cytokine expression (TNF-α and IL-6) in in vivo animal and human models of sepsis.
35167625.what_it_found: The study found differences in the timing of IRAK3 mRNA peak expression between humans and rodents, and observed similarities in TNF-α and IL-6 protein expression patterns between human and rodent in vivo models, though human cytokine levels decreased more rapidly.

key_quotes.quote: Meta-analyses of in vivo studies further confirmed the roles of IRAK3 during immunosuppression phase of sepsis.
IRAK3 mRNA expression in humans reached peak levels at IT following one-challenge, and this is earlier than in mice at LT (Fig 2) [38, 45].
Patterns of TNF-α and IL-6 expression in human in vivo models are more similar to mice in vivo models than in vitro cell culture (Figs 3 and S1 and S2) [46].
However, the protein levels of IL-6 and TNF-α reported in included human in vivo studies were still in the value ranges of clinical samples of patients with sepsis or septic shock (Fig 3) [18, 19].

The inhibitory effect of IRAK3 following two-challenges was confirmed with meta-analyses by both in vivo and in vitro studies, and correlates to clinical outcomes, indicating the importance of IRAK3 in immunosuppression phase of sepsis.
There is a shortage of human in vivo studies investigating how IRAK3 expression influences immune outcomes, especially for two-challenge intervention.

34127759.what_the_study_did: The study compared the cellular and molecular features of inflammation in tenocytes from humans and four animal models (mouse, rat, sheep, horse) to evaluate their suitability as translational models for tendon research.
34127759.what_it_found: No single animal model perfectly replicates human tenocyte behavior and response to inflammation, with each model showing similarities and differences across various aspects like proliferation, migration, and gene expression.

key_quotes.quote: No animal model sufficiently emulates human tenocytes’ cellular and molecular features and response to inflammation to be considered the gold-standard for tendon research.

Translational medicine will need to continue to rely on a fit-for-purpose selection of animal models to approximate the human condition, based on the essential characteristics that must be mimicked for a particular research question.
Peculiarities, strengths, and weaknesses of the model species need to be accounted for in the study design, analysis and interpretation.
Data from multiple animal models should be combined to optimize translational predictive validity.
The species show variable approximations of human expression levels among functional gene groups and conditions.
The overall gene expression of human tenocytes was most similar to murine under healthy, equine under transient and ovine under constant inflammatory conditions.

34916915.what_the_study_did: This study discusses how combining animal welfare with experimental rigor can improve reproducibility in behavioral neuroscience, focusing on aspects like understanding animal models, using suitable statistical methods, and environmental enrichment.
34916915.what_it_found: The study argues that adherence to regulations, proper experimental design, personnel training, and environmental enrichment can lead to higher quality and more reproducible behavioral neuroscience studies.

key_quotes.quote: The currently available empirical estimates on the topic suggest that less than half (ranging from 49% down to 11%) of scientific results are reproducible.
In our opinion, combining principles of animal welfare with experimental rigor may lead to improvement in the quality of studies in behavioral neuroscience.
There is evidence that “happy animals make better science”.

By definition, a model is a construct of a real physical component or property observed in nature. Therefore, a model is always imperfect and does not contemplate the full complexity of the real system that is being modeled.
Limited knowledge of the scientific method and statistics are among the reasons for the high levels of experimental bias and irreproducibility.

A common non-tested argument to raise research animals in impoverished standard conditions is that the data variability among laboratories, or even within them, would increase by raising the animals in enriched non-standard conditions.

measurements.measures: the overall similarity between dog and human cancers, with lower scores indicating less similarity
measurements.compared: dog cancers vs human cancers
measurements.verbatim: Overall, the cancer rankings derived using our formula match findings identified by previous studies in individual cancers not included among positive controls, such as pediatric GBM/LGG [46] and OS [20, 31], as well as adult HNSC [71, 72], SARC [25, 26], and PRAD [73], suggesting that our formula accurately quantifies overall model robustness for specific cancers. All positive controls scored above 70% with the exception of adult DLBC, however all still scored higher than the negative controls. We also provide scores for understudied dog cancer types, for which similarities can be inferred based on their relative positioning within the spectrum of cancers. When considering all cancers and given the variability in scores, we recommend caution in the use of dogs to model some of these human cancers. Lower-scoring cancers, such as pediatric SKCM, might be better suited for mechanistic studies rather than as a wholistic natural model. Overall, findings from our quantitative formula of model robustness highlight that researchers should prioritize dog models with consistently high composite scores for hypothesis testing and drug evaluation.

42245789.what_the_study_did: The study performed a pancancer analysis of 5,875 samples (913 dogs and 4,962 human samples) spanning 11 tumor types to quantify transcriptomic similarities between human and dog cancers.
42245789.what_it_found: Overall, dogs are an excellent model for many human cancers and tend to be better models of adult cancers than pediatric cancers, with notable exceptions.

key_quotes.quote: We show that, overall, dogs are an excellent model for many human cancers and that dogs tend to be better models of adult cancers than pediatric cancers, with notable exceptions such as gliomas and sarcomas.
Our scalable approach enables rapid and accurate identification of model systems for studying human cancers, creating new opportunities for comparative oncology studies across the tree of life.
Dogs develop spontaneous tumors that closely resemble human tumors, have a high tumor incidence rate, and their popularity as pets ensures the wide availability of samples for scientific studies.
Dog tumors, however, are not universally strong models of human tumors.

Critically, we identify that clustering metrics better describe similarities between transcriptomic profiles of dog and human tumors than previously applied differential expression approaches, as they take into account tumor type heterogeneity.
When considering all cancers and given the variability in scores, we recommend caution in the use of dogs to model some of these human cancers.

38676802.what_the_study_did: This study is a compilation of methods and protocols for using patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) in cancer research and drug development.
38676802.what_it_found: PDXs are valuable preclinical models that closely mimic human tumors, aiding in understanding cancer biology, identifying biomarkers, screening drugs, and advancing personalized medicine, despite facing challenges such as metastatic potential variability and stromal changes.

key_quotes.quote: Patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) represent a critical advancement in preclinical cancer research, wherein human tumor samples are implanted into animal models for evaluation of therapeutic responses.
PDXs have emerged as indispensable tools in translational cancer research, facilitating investigation into tumor microenvironments and personalized medicine.

Evidently, these models have demonstrated inadequate predictive ability in terms of clinical outcomes, with a staggering 90% of potential therapeutics that pass preclinical stages failing in human trials due to inefficacy [52, 53].

PDXs provide a biologically stable and precise reflection of the patient’s tumor, including gene transcription, epigenetic modulations, genetic variation, histopathology, inflammation, and circumstances of responses toward treatments [9].

PDXs have become a cornerstone of cancer research, offering insights into mechanobiology, metastasis, tumorigenesis, and the preclinical evaluation of anticancer therapies with the goal of advancing personalized cancer treatment strategies.

Despite their many advantages, PDX models present certain challenges. For example, when modeling for late stages of cancer, PDX tumors may fail to fully metastasize, as seen in breast cancer PDXs that commonly only metastasize to lymph nodes and lungs, despite patients also showing brain and bone metastasizes [48].

38867022.what_the_study_did: The study retrospectively analyzed and ranked commonly used murine models for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) based on their similarity to human MASLD.

key_quotes.quote: The lack of a standard translationally relevant preclinical model has hindered the field’s ability to study the chronic and complex pathophysiology of MASH.

Disappointingly, within each diet macro-category, relatively subtle differences in micronutrient and macronutrient composition (for example, amount of cholesterol or choline) and study designs are sufficient to introduce variability in MASLD disease endpoints.

Our approach identified murine MASLD models showing (phenotypic and/or histologic and/or transcriptomic) profiles relevant to human MASH, which are suitable for most preclinical experimental applications.
Murine MASLD transcriptomes are close to humans but do not predict fibrosis efficiently.

This analysis indicates that despite variations in specific single gene expression, the biological pathways implicated in the disease were consistently regulated across both the animal models and human cases.

Our study provides several important outcomes and unique insights. A key strength of our study lies in the uniformity of methodology applied across all models for staining and scoring liver histopathology.

measurements.measures: correlation between the standard deviation of mutation rates between PDXs and patient tumors
measurements.compared: PDX mutation rate standard deviation vs. patient tumor mutation rate standard deviation
measurements.verbatim: The median mutation rate showed a weaker correlation between cell lines and patient tumors, primarily because of a lack of hypermutators in melanoma cell line models. Specifically, 75/121 (62%) of TCGA samples have a mutation rate higher than 10 per megabase, compared to 23/44 (52%) of PDXE models and 13/49 (27%) of CCLE cell lines. All other lineages have a higher median mutation rate in cell lines than in primary tumors, possibly because of bias introduced by the amenability of tumors to growing on plastic or because post-somatic mutations accrue in cell lines during passaging. PDXE samples have a much smaller increased mutation rate (probably because of residual unfiltered germline variants) and s.d., which is consistent with less divergence from the patient tumors.

26479923.what_the_study_did: The study established approximately 1,000 patient-derived tumor xenograft (PDX) models and performed in vivo compound screens using a 1x1x1 experimental design (PDX clinical trial or PCT) to assess population responses to 62 treatments across six indications.
26479923.what_it_found: The study demonstrated the reproducibility and clinical translatability of the PDX-based approach, identifying associations between genotype and drug response, and established mechanisms of resistance, suggesting PCTs may be more accurate than cell line models for assessing clinical potential.

key_quotes.quote: Roughly 85% of preclinical agents entering oncology clinical trials fail to demonstrate sufficient safety or efficacy to gain regulatory approval1–3.

Increasing amounts of evidence have suggested that PDXs faithfully recapitulate human tumor biology and predict patient drug response (reviewed by Tentler et al.5, Siolas and Hannon6, Rosfjord et al.7 and Hidalgo et al.8) by directly comparing drug responses in patients and their corresponding xenografts.
Our results suggest that PCTs may represent a more accurate approach than cell line models for assessing the clinical potential of some therapeutic modalities.

The frequency of genetic alterations across the three data sets was remarkably consistent; however, we see greater correspondence between PDX models and clinical samples than between the CCLE models and clinical samples.
These data strongly suggest that PDXs and PCTs are well-suited tools for discovering mechanisms of resistance.

To our knowledge, the herein described PDX clinical trial concept is the first to evaluate the reproducibility and translatability of the 1 × 1 × 1 concept to drug response using an extensive, wellcharacterized PDX collection.

27261415.what_the_study_did: The study developed and characterized a diet-induced mouse model (DIAMOND) for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and hepatocellular cancer (HCC).
27261415.what_it_found: The DIAMOND model, using a specific mouse strain and diet, successfully recapitulated key features of human NAFLD, including steatosis, steatohepatitis, progressive fibrosis, and HCC, with transcriptomic similarities to human disease.

key_quotes.quote: A strong concordance of the mouse gene expression patterns at 8 and 52 weeks to the human NASH transcriptome was observed (FDR 0.02 and 0.08, respectively) ( Fig. 5E ).

When compared to human cirrhosis of varied etiologies including NASH (186-gene signature, including 73 poor prognosis-correlated and 113 good prognosis-correlated genes) [ 23 , 24 ], the pattern of gene expression within the mouse transcriptome at 52 weeks demonstrated significant concordance with cirrhosis of poor prognosis (FDR <0.001) ( Fig. 5F ).
HCC developed in 89% of mice between weeks 32–52.
Histologically, the ballooning, Mallory-Denk bodies and apoptotic cells were as typically described in the literature and comparable to human NASH ( Figs. 2D and 3 ).

Collectively, these results indicate that the crossed mouse background B6/129 fed a WD SW constitute a faster and more powerful model than the pure B6 mouse to recreate all biochemical and histological parameters and HCC development as seen in human NASH.
A large proportion of the mice developed spontaneous HCC while it is known that only a small proportion of afflicted humans develop HCC [ 31 ].

32631250.what_the_study_did: The study compared liver histopathological and transcriptome characteristics in GAN diet-induced obese mice (GAN DIO-NASH) with human NASH patients to assess the clinical translatability of the mouse model.
32631250.what_it_found: The GAN DIO-NASH mouse model showed significant clinical translatability with respect to histopathological, transcriptional, and metabolic aspects of human NASH, demonstrating similar disease hallmarks and gene expression patterns.

key_quotes.quote: The main findings were significant clinical translatability of the GAN DIO-NASH mouse model with respect to the histopathological, transcriptional and metabolic aspects of human NASH.
GAN DIO-NASH mice showed similar morphological appearance of steatosis, inflammatory foci and hepatocyte ballooning as compared to human NASH.
Overlapping hepatic transcriptome profiles in GAN DIO-NASH mice and NASH patients.
GAN DIO-NASH mice demonstrated significantly increased levels of plasma biomarkers known to be relevant to NAFLD/NASH diagnosis and assessment of fibrosis risk.

GAN DIO-NASH mice develop characteristics of the metabolic syndrome indicated by obesity, hypercholesterolemia and hyperinsulinemia with impaired glucose tolerance, the latter being a central feature of insulin resistance.

The GAN DIO-NASH mouse demonstrates good clinical translatability with respect to the physiological, metabolic and histopathological aspects of fibrosing NASH along with a strong concordance with the liver transcriptome signature of the human disease.

29302222.what_the_study_did: This study reviews the utility of animal models in addiction research, discussing their face, construct, and predictive validity in relation to human addiction.
29302222.what_it_found: Animal models, particularly those based on self-administration, incubation of craving, and relapse, show promise in understanding addiction mechanisms and developing treatments, with rats often being a preferred model over mice due to better translational potential.

key_quotes.quote: The precondition for each animal model is a high degree of face validity, defined here as characteristic behavioral features that are seen both in laboratory animals and in humans.

Consequently, self-administration-based animal models are helpful in unraveling the molecular and neurobiological mechanisms of drug-related behaviors and therefore critical in identifying strategies useful in the intervention of human drug consumption; ie, they provide predictive validity.

It is remarkable that the incubation phenomenon of drug seeking was first discovered in laboratory rats and later also demonstrated to occur in smokers, 43 alcoholics, 44 and cocaine addicts 45 —such a direct translation to the human situation indicates high face, construct, and predictive validity of the incubation model of drug craving.

In alcoholics, medications that reduce relapse rates, such as naltrexone and acamprosate, also reduce compulsive drinking during an ADE, 58 , 59 demonstrating the predictive power of this animal model.

For example, glutamate spectroscopy in alcohol-dependent rats and alcohol-dependent humans has yielded identical results: during withdrawal, both rats and humans demonstrate hyperglutamatergic activity in different brain sites that diminishes when withdrawal symptomatology subsides. 73

40558535.what_the_study_did: This study reviews the genetic and environmental risk factors for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and how they are modeled in animal and human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived models.
40558535.what_it_found: The study highlights the strengths and weaknesses of various ASD models, advocating for orthogonal validation across different model systems and cautioning against overstating the conclusions from any single model.

key_quotes.quote: While these models have contributed to a wealth of studies that have significantly expanded our understanding of ASD, animal models present with some inherent limitations to translatability, such as their inability to recapitulate human-specific transcriptional paradigms and the protracted development of the human brain.
Over the last decade, human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived 2D models such as induced neurons (iNs) as well as 3D models (organoids, assembloids) have started to bridge this gap.
A perfect animal model of ASD is untenable because autism, especially facets of it that arise at the interface of developmental gene expression programs and neuronal circuits, is human specific.
NHP ASD models resemble humans in both structural and molecular features of brain organization.
Shank3 KO exhibits increased penetrance in cynomolgus monkeys compared to multiple mouse models, and the KO monkeys match the human condition more closely than mice.
To this day, a perfect ASD model does not exist.

35781406.what_the_study_did: The study established patient-derived tumor xenografts (PDTX) from sarcoma patient tumors and compared the efficacy of drug regimens tested on these xenografts with the actual responses of the patients to those same regimens.
35781406.what_it_found: The PDTX model demonstrated a 100% concordance with patient responses for 17 tested regimens, suggesting high accuracy in predicting drug efficacy for sarcoma treatment.

key_quotes.quote: Histopathological examination showed a 100% consistency between primary tumours and tumour grafts.
The overall success rate of engraftment was 73.8% (31/42).
The concordance between the patients’ responses and PDTX predictions was 100%.
The most effective regimen was the combination of docetaxel and gemcitabine, with a response rate of 9/12.
Apatinib, an anti-angiogenesis agent, had the worst response rate, with only one patient responding.

PDTX is an ideal preclinical model for sarcomas because of its faithful preservation of the heterogeneity of the disease, a satisfactory engraftment rate and high accuracy in its prediction of drug efﬁcacy.

31694927.what_the_study_did: The study developed and characterized species-specific Liver-Chips (rat, dog, and human) using microengineered organs-on-chips technology to evaluate drug-induced liver toxicity.
31694927.what_it_found: The Liver-Chip models demonstrated the ability to recapitulate species-specific drug toxicities, identify mechanisms of toxicity, and predict human relevance of liver toxicities observed in animal studies.

key_quotes.quote: An analysis of 150 drugs that caused adverse events in humans found that regulatory testing in rats and dogs correctly predicted just 71% of toxicities in humans (1).

Moreover, whereas gastrointestinal, hematological, and cardiovascular toxicities were predicted with a relatively high concordance, the ability to predict drug-induced liver injury (DILI) was much lower.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency generally require the safety of new drug candidates to be evaluated in both rodent and nonrodent animal models, frequently rat and dog, before moving the new chemical entity into human clinical trials.

A multispecies Liver-Chip may provide a useful platform for prediction of liver toxicity and inform human relevance of liver toxicities detected in animal studies to better determine safety and human risk.

These results suggest that a species-specific Liver-Chip can be used to predict rat, dog, and human hepatotoxicities and that they may be useful for safety and risk assessment to estimate human relevance of drug-induced liver toxicities seen in animals.
They could also potentially be used to predict human idiosyncratic hepatotoxicities and elucidate mechanisms of action.

39255793.what_the_study_did: The study developed and validated PTMoreR, a tool for cross-species PTM mapping, and applied it to analyze phosphoproteomes across mammals and in specific clades, as well as to integrate PTM data with protein-protein interactions.
39255793.what_it_found: PTMoreR enables motif-centric cross-species PTM analysis, revealing conserved and divergent phosphorylation patterns across mammalian evolution and facilitating comparative phosphoproteomics.

key_quotes.quote: As the first validation step assessing the general usage of PTMoreR in mapping and functionally annotating PTM sites from another species to human, we performed a cross-species analysis on mouse and human phosphoproteomes; both have been extensively measured by high-throughput MS-based phosphoproteomics.
We found that using simple aa similarity scores ≥8, a total of 87,716 P-sites experimentally identified in human were successfully mapped to the corresponding sites in the mouse sequence.
We thus argue that the constitutions of many other mammalian species’ phosphoproteomes could be largely inferred in a similar manner.
Using PTMoreR, we extracted the unique, confidently localized P-sites and blasted these phosphopeptide sequences from non-human species to human sequences.
PTMoreR mapped a total of 8,582 phosphopeptides to corresponding Human homolog sites and supported motif enrichment analysis and KS annotation in Vero E6 cells (Figures 7, S5 C, and S5D).

Our comparison essentially only characterizes the evolution of human P-sites, which naturally ignores the possible kinases uniquely present in other mammalian kinomes or newly emerged KS relationships that bestow a phenotypic advantage over time for a given species.

40849367.what_the_study_did: The study adapted probabilistic reversal learning (PRL) tasks for humans and rats, recorded EEG during task performance, and applied computational models to compare behavioral, computational, and neurophysiological markers of cognitive flexibility across species.
40849367.what_it_found: The study found remarkably concordant behavioral, computational, and electrophysiological markers of cognitive flexibility between humans and rats, including a reward positivity (RewP) neurophysiological response.

key_quotes.quote: we identified behavioral, computational, and neurophysiological markers of cognitive flexibility that were similar across species, providing a robust platform that could hasten treatment development.

Behavioral performance between species was comparable, as indicated by greater sensitivity to positive feedback (i.e., target win-stay) relative to negative feedback (i.e., target lose-shift), both of which significantly correlated with the overall number of reversals in both species.

Q-learning computational analyses revealed that both humans and rats assigned greater value to target vs. non-target stimuli, and these values alternated between response apertures as the criterion for reversals was achieved and reward contingencies were switched.
These results suggest that the frontal voltage changes triggered by reward feedback represent a neural marker of PEs that is consistent across humans and rats.

Notably, in both species (Fig. 3 A, B ), the regression coefficient peaked in the time window corresponding to the RewP. This indicates that during the RewP period, greater ERP/LFP amplitudes are associated with more positive PEs, whereas lower ERP/LFP amplitudes are associated with less positive PEs.

The absence of this effect in humans suggests that the maximal human dose administered (200 mg) was not sufficient to disrupt behavior and neurophysiology in a manner consistent with that observed in rats.

39182537.what_the_study_did: This study investigated functional connectivity (FC) changes in the brains of human patients with thalamic pain and a macaque model of thalamic pain to identify cross-species convergence.
39182537.what_it_found: The study found convergent increases in functional connectivity between the amygdala and brainstem regions (specifically the basolateral amygdala and ventral tegmental area/midbrain) in both human patients and macaques with thalamic pain. Additionally, increased FC between the amygdala and the mediodorsal thalamus was observed in both species.

key_quotes.quote: The present results suggest that the FC changes in the regions associated with emotion, memory, motivation, and reward are part of the underlying mechanisms of thalamic pain onset present in both human patients and model macaques.
This cross-species convergence provides new insights into the neurological mechanisms underlying thalamic pain, paving the way for further studies and the development of therapeutic strategies.
In humans, the FC between the amygdala on the nonaffected side and the brainstem, specifically between the BLA and VTA, significantly increased in the thalamic pain condition.
A macaque model of thalamic pain mirrored these results with increased FC between the amygdala on the nonaffected side and brainstem, and more specifically between the BLA and midbrain.

Conversely, a significant pain-related increase in FC between the amygdala and MD, which was the most prominent FC change observed in the macaque model of thalamic pain (Fig 7), was also reproduced in human patients.
The present study showing the cross-species convergence of the pain-related FC changes advances our understanding of the causality of thalamic pain in human patients using a macaque model.

25671556.what_it_found: Dog models have been critical in advancing gene therapy for inherited retinal diseases to clinical trials, showing promise but also highlighting species-specific differences in outcomes.

key_quotes.quote: Despite the safe and encouraging improvement in visual function, the degree of rescue achieved in human patients has been nowhere near that achieved in the preclinical Rpe65- mutant dog trials.
In contrast, in dogs there is a remarkable improvement in the ERG, indicating restoration of function close to normal levels (Fig. 1).
Vision in dogs after treatment appears very close to normal, while human patients remain visually impaired.

One major reason is that human patients have a much faster relative decline in photoreceptor numbers compared with dogs and invariably already have a marked loss of photoreceptors when treated, whereas the dogs treated up to middle age have good preservation of photoreceptors that respond well to restoration of visual cycle function.

26563791.what_the_study_did: This chapter reviews animal models used to study neurotoxicity targeting the extrapyramidal system, focusing on similarities and differences with human responses.
26563791.what_it_found: Animal models can replicate various aspects of human neurotoxic syndromes affecting the extrapyramidal system, but often with species-specific differences and incomplete replication of all human features.

key_quotes.quote: One goal of this chapter is to illustrate the similarity in responses seen in animals and people.

Rodents generally fail to develop a behavioral syndrome or neuropathologic lesion comparable to that seen in manganese-poisoned humans. In contrast, nonhuman primates best replicate the neurotoxic effects observed in humans.

MPTP produces a syndrome that replicates most of the clinical signs of MPTP neurotoxicity in humans, including clinical signs (e.g., akinesia, rigidity, postural tremor, flexed posture), dopamine depletion, responsiveness to L-DOPA treatment, and neuropathology (e.g., dopaminergic neuronal loss in the substantia nigra pars compacta).

Despite the limitations some animal-toxicant models have shown for human neurodegenerative disease, the toxicology community should not lose sight of the fact that they are still useful tools for the study of chemical neurotoxicity.
The choice of the animal model to be used rests on the research question(s) being evaluated.

Gwiazda et al.’s (2007) review of subchronic to chronic rodent and nonhuman primate studies led them to conclude that most existing animal studies might be of limited relevance for the risk assessment of chronic low-level manganese exposure to humans.

11029269.what_the_study_did: This study analyzed a database of human toxicities (HTs) identified during pharmaceutical development to determine how well animal toxicity studies predicted these human toxicities.
11029269.what_it_found: The study found a true positive concordance rate of 71% for human toxicities being predicted by animal models, with nonrodent species being more predictive than rodent species.

key_quotes.quote: The results showed the true positive HT concordance rate of 71% for rodent and nonrodent species, with nonrodents alone being predictive for 63% of HTs and rodents alone for 43%.
Where animal models, in one or more species, identified concordant HT, 94% were first observed in studies of 1 month or less in duration.

Overall, the true positive concordance rate (sensitivity) was 70% for one or more preclinical animal model species (either in safety pharmacology or in safety toxicology) showing target organ toxicity in the same organ system as the HT (Fig. 3).
Concordance was seen in 63% of nonrodent studies (primarily the dog) and 43% of rodent studies (primarily the rat).
The main finding of this study is the true positive concordance rate of over 71% for comparable target organs in animal toxicity studies for identified HTs.

A significant message from this survey is that the two HTs with the poorest correlation with animal studies (liver and hypersensitivity/cutaneous reactions) were also the two HTs that led most often to termination of clinical development.

28422076.what_the_study_did: The study developed and validated the ZeGlobalTox assay, an innovative experimental procedure using zebrafish larvae to assess organ-specific drug toxicity (cardio-, neuro-, and hepatotoxicity) as a proxy to predict human organ toxicity.
28422076.what_it_found: The ZeGlobalTox assay demonstrated high predictive potential, achieving 89% specificity, 68% sensitivity, and 78% accuracy in predicting human toxicity, reinforcing the utility of zebrafish as a model for early drug safety assessment.

key_quotes.quote: We will show that by using ZeGlobaltox, a high toxicity predictivity is achieved—specificity (89%), sensitivity (68%), and accuracy (78%).

These results reinforce the validation of zebrafish as a suitable model for pre-mammalian studies to reduce and/or replace mammalian vertebrate usage, experimental time, and cost during the process of drug discovery and development.
Results obtained through the ZeGlobalTox assay show high sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy values when we compare the zebrafish experimental data with known human toxicity outputs ( Table 3 ).

However, our experimental methodology—drug exposure timing, chosen drug concentration, image acquisition, and image analysis—might require some further improvement to facilitate a more accurate detection of some of the analysed parameters.
On the other hand, better sensitivity is indeed required because five compounds known to produce some kind of neurotoxicity in humans did not alter larvae locomotion significantly.

In that regard, zebrafish could become the chosen model to bridge the gap between low predictive but high throughput in vitro studies and high predictive but expensive and time-consuming in vivo mammalian studies.

35148401.what_the_study_did: The study assessed the concordance between nonclinical repolarization assays and clinical QT interval prolongation by analyzing literature and a joint HESI/FDA database of drug applications.
35148401.what_it_found: There is a strong qualitative concordance between human and nonrodent animal QT results, with high percentages of drugs showing similar QT prolongation effects. However, a notable percentage of drugs showed discordance, highlighting challenges in predicting human outcomes from animal models.

key_quotes.quote: The search found that, in the last 51 years of published scientific literature, there was a strong qualitative concordance between QT results found in humans and QT results in nonrodent animal studies.

Vargas et al. (2015) found that 91% of the drugs that prolonged the QT interval in humans also did so in animals and 88% of drugs that did not prolong the QT in humans had no effect on animals ( Tables 1 and 2 ).

A lack of concordance did occur for approximately10% of drugs evaluated, and there appeared to be plausible explanations for the underlying disconnect between the human and nonrodent animal QT outcomes ( Vargas et al. , 2015 ).
Overall concordance in the database was moderate, and out of 150 drugs evaluated, a total of 47 (31%) were found to be discordant based on a predetermined definition.

The retrospective analysis of 150 submitted drug applications demonstrated robust specificity (the ability to identify drugs without clinical QTc prolongation) but poor sensitivity (the ability to identify drugs with clinical QTc prolongation) when nonclinical assays were used.
The in vivo QTc assay provided more robust positive and negative predictive values compared with the in vitro assays.

23812503.what_the_study_did: The study developed and evaluated logistic regression models to predict torsade de pointes (TdP) risk using ion channel block data, comparing models based on hERG channel block alone versus models incorporating multiple ion channel effects (MICE).
23812503.what_it_found: Models incorporating multiple ion channel effects (MICE) significantly improved the prediction of TdP risk compared to models based solely on hERG channel block.

key_quotes.quote: Models using MICE variables significantly improved TdP predictivity.
Model 5 correctly identified verapamil as non-torsadogenic (P(+TdP) = 0.31) and terfenadine as torsadogenic (P(+TdP) = 0.97).
Compared to Model 1, false positives were halved and false negatives reduced six-fold.
This study confirms our hypothesis that Models based on MICE more accurately predict torsadogenic potential than Models based on hERG effects alone.

The MICE assay is not only better than the hERG assay but, the fact that it uses automated patch clamp instruments, provides higher throughput and faster turn-around times than the manually performed patch clamp method.
This study demonstrates that TdP risk can be accurately assessed using MICE early in the development process.

38852684.what_the_study_did: The study developed and validated a method for analyzing the concentration-QTc relationship in preclinical animal models using sparse pharmacokinetic data.
38852684.what_it_found: The proposed method accurately predicts QTc changes in animals based on drug concentration, correlating well with human data, and can be applied even with non-simultaneous PK and QTc measurements.

key_quotes.quote: In NHP, a 10.9 ± 0.06 ms (mean ± 95% CI) change in QTc was detected at approximately 1.5× the moxifloxacin plasma concentration that causes a 10 ms QTc change in humans, based on a 0-24 h super-interval.
Similarly, in canines, a 16.6 ± 0.1 ms change was detected at 1.7× critical clinical moxifloxacin concentration, and a 0.04 ± 0.1 ms change was seen for mock.
While simultaneous PK and QTc data points are preferred, practical constraints and the need for QTc averaging did not prevent concentration-QTc analyses.
Utilizing a 0-24 h super-interval method illustrates a simple and effective method to address cardiovascular questions when preclinical drug exposures exceed clinical concentrations.
Previous studies have confirmed that canine and NHP studies may be useful for predicting human outcomes.
Humans, however, are more sensitive, with their maximum probability of a QTc prolonging effect occurring at lower concentrations than in NHP and canine.

40863351.what_the_study_did: The study evaluated the cardiotoxic effects of vanoxerine using two nonclinical human cardiac new approach methodologies (NAMs): a complex cardiac microphysiological system (MPS) and a human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (hiPSC-CM) multielectrode array (MEA) Comprehensive in vitro proarrhythmia assay (CiPA) model.
40863351.what_it_found: The study demonstrated that both cardiac NAMs could predict vanoxerine-induced Torsades de Pointes (TdP) proarrhythmic risk categorization in vitro, with vanoxerine treatment delaying repolarization and inducing early afterdepolarizations (EADs) independently of cardiac structural damage.

key_quotes.quote: These findings demonstrate cardiac NAMs have the potential to be used for safety and efficacy assessment with the advantage of minimizing the use of animal models.
Our report is the first study that systematically quantifies vanoxerine proarrhythmia (i.e., TdP) potential in multiple cardiac NAMs.

The cardiac MPS utilizes a triple parametric approach employing hiPSC-CM to model human cardiac function with enhanced physiological relevance and predictive power by capturing the full EC coupling cascade.

The TdP risk categorization models in combination with hiPSC-CMs create a physiologically relevant platform that may fill the unmet needs of current models to predict drug-induced cardiovascular liability before clinical presentation and assist regulatory decision-making.
In this study, independent application of two mechanistically distinct models allows for greater confidence in the in vitro assessment of vanoxerine’s pro-arrhythmogenic potential.

Taken together, the current study demonstrates that nonclinical cardiac NAMs can recapitulate clinical outcomes and predict vanoxerine-induced delayed repolarization and TdP risk categorization in vitro.

20807552.what_the_study_did: This study retrospectively compared hERG current assay performance with drug-induced QTc prolongation from clinical studies for 39 drugs to evaluate the utility and limitations of the hERG assay in predicting clinical outcomes.
20807552.what_it_found: A hERG safety margin of 45 provided optimal performance in linking safety margins to QTc prolongation, with sensitivity of 0.64 and specificity of 0.88. Likelihood ratios indicated that QTc prolonging drugs are 5-7 times more likely to have low safety margins (1-30 range).

key_quotes.quote: Based on receiver–operator characteristics, a hERG safety margin of 45 provided optimal overall performance linking safety margins to QTc prolongation (sensitivity (true positive rate) = 0.64, speciﬁcity (true negative rate) = 0.88); the area under the receiver–operator curve (0.72) is indicative of moderate overall concordance.

Likelihood ratios calculated from multitier contingency tables suggest that QTc prolonging drugs are only 5–7 times as likely to demonstrate low safety margins (1–30 range) compared to drugs that do not prolong QTc.
key_quotes.topic: Likelihood ratios for low safety margins

key_quotes.quote: Paradoxically, higher safety margins demonstrate lesser conﬁdence predicting prolongation.

The overall limitations of hERG safety margins shown using these quantitative, evidencebased approaches highlight the need for additional preclinical assays and adaptive strategies throughout drug discovery to reliably mitigate QTc prolongation risk.

While drugs with higher safety margin values generally demonstrated less QTc prolongation (point estimated less than 5 ms), each category contained at least one drug that elicited QTc prolongation N 5 ms.

Relatively low sensitivity and likelihood ratio values highlight the need to clarify delayed repolarization risk further with additional preclinical assays and adaptive strategies to avoid unwarranted compound attrition.

33813006.what_the_study_did: The study evaluated the utility of the core battery of safety pharmacology studies used to support first-in-human clinical entry of 105 small molecule drug candidates over a decade.
33813006.what_it_found: The study found that routine use of rodent CNS and respiratory function tests has limited utility, a stand-alone hERG assay is not sensitive in predicting proarrhythmic risk, and routine use of conscious animal telemetry studies may not be necessary as a default.

key_quotes.quote: Routine use of the latter 2 studies appears to have limited utility, with only 21% and 28% of studies, respectively, giving findings of which none were identified as of obvious concern to moving the affected drugs into the clinic.
The use of a stand-alone hERG assay does not appear to be particular sensitive in predicting proarrythmic risk as a tool by itself.

Telemetry study testing had utility especially for identifying effects on QTc interval (about 10% of studies), resulting on some occasions in a lower clinical starting dose and/or increased awareness for potential effects on the cardiovascular system in the Phase I study.
Overall, this investigation provides information supporting an overhaul of the current “box ticking” core battery approach used for safety pharmacology testing.

From an evaluation of 141 small molecules from 5 pharma companies, it was shown that headache (52%), nausea (38%), dizziness (36%), fatigue/somnolence (33%) and pain (15%) seen were clinically but that Irwin/FOB testing did not predict these 5 adverse events (i.e., did not provide value in terms of detecting occurrence).

In looking at the overall predictive value and discriminatory power of a combination of hERG and in vivo QT assays based on a collection of 200 nonclinical-clinical data sets, it was indicated that a compound that is considered negative in both these tests has a very low probability of QTc prolongation (3.8%) and torsades de pointes risk (TdP) (<0.1%) regardless of the outcome of the clinical testing.

30726989.what_the_study_did: The study investigated the translation of heart rate (HR) and blood pressure (BP) endpoints from preclinical animal models (rat and large animal) to human clinical trials.
30726989.what_it_found: Cardiovascular safety endpoints (HR and BP) show good concordance between rat and large animal models, and between large animal models and human clinical trials, with effects generally translating within a 0.3-3 fold range of free plasma concentration.

key_quotes.quote: The rat CV model showed good concordance (sensitivity = 84% and specificity = 71%) for LA BP and HR changes.
Similarly, LA CV measures of HR and BP showed good concordance (sensitivity = 78% and specificity = 79%) to clinical changes.
Directionality of BP and HR change was conserved between LA to humans.
However, for rat to LA comparisons the directionality of change was opposite for 23% – 26% compounds.
For rat to LA translation, PPV and NPV values for the combined BP/HR endpoint were 90% and 60%, respectively.
For the LA to human translation, the PPV and NPV were 52% and 92%, respectively, for the combined BP/HR endpoint.

26753942.what_the_study_did: The study analyzed data from over 3,000 drugs to assess the predictive value of animal tests for human drug toxicity, using Likelihood Ratios (LRs) to measure evidential weight.
26753942.what_it_found: Animal tests provide little to no evidential weight for predicting human drug toxicity, especially when toxicity is absent in animals. The predictive value varies significantly between species and drug classes.

key_quotes.quote: Our results for species including humans, NHPs, dogs, mice, rabbits, and rats, have major implications for the value of animal tests in predicting human toxicity, and demand that human-focused alternative methods are adopted in their place as a matter of urgency.
the absence of toxicity in animals provides essentially no insight into the likelihood of toxicity or absence of toxicity in humans.

Crucially, median iNLRs were substantially lower than PLRs, and were barely greater than unity, supporting the view that, when toxicity appears to be absent in one species, this result provides essentially no evidential weight to the likelihood of lack of toxicity in any other species.

While the presence of toxicity in one species may sometimes add evidential weight for risk of toxicity in another, the LRs are extremely inconsistent, varying substantially for different classes of drugs and their effects.

It is increasingly clear that the animal testing of human drugs is not fit-for-purpose, and this is especially true in the light of the astounding array of directly human-relevant methods now available to science for testing new drugs.

At the very least, the fact that there is conflicting evidence in this respect, and that our analyses are, necessarily, based on the relatively limited publicly-available data, demands that further analyses of proprietary data, conducted and/or overseen by industry, are conducted in a transparent, and preferably independent, manner.

30364994.what_the_study_did: The study constructed a 3D human gastrointestinal microtissue and evaluated its ability to predict drug-induced diarrhea by measuring transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER).
30364994.what_it_found: The human GI microtissue TEER assay demonstrated a predictive accuracy of 83-84% for clinical diarrhea, outperforming MTT assays and Caco-2 cell TEER assays, and showed potential for informing mathematical models of drug toxicity.

key_quotes.quote: Retrospective evaluation of compounds with clinical GI toxicity (100% prevalence), revealed that GIT in rodents had only 46% clinical concordance compared with 83% in nonrodents (Olson et al., 2000).

Conversely, when compounds with preclinical GIT were followed prospectively through the completion of Phase 1 trials, the diagnostic value of different species revealed a proportionate reduction in uncertainty of 15% and 28% in rat and dog respectively compared with 87% in primate studies (Monticello et al., 2017).
The predictive accuracy of the initial and repeat experiments were 84% and 83%, respectively (Tables 3 and 4).
MTT yielded a 70% accuracy but only 50% sensitivity (Table 4).

The validation set was also tested on Caco-2 cells where TEER responses exhibited 77% accuracy but only 57% sensitivity (Table 4); performance insufficient to meet standards for drug screening (Genschow et al., 2002).
The data revealed a predictive accuracy of 80% which matches the translation accuracy of in vivo studies in higher-order species (Monticello et al., 2017; Olson et al., 2000).

27870924.what_the_study_did: The study conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of preclinical in vivo animal models of sepsis to evaluate the efficacy of mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) therapy prior to initiating a first-in-human trial.
27870924.what_it_found: MSC therapy significantly reduced the odds of death in preclinical animal models of sepsis, with the effect size remaining robust across various experimental conditions, although potential threats to validity such as publication bias and methodological weaknesses were identified.

key_quotes.quote: MSC therapy in preclinical models of sepsis significantly reduced the overall odds of death (odds ratio (OR) 0.27, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.18–0.40 ( Figure 2 ).

Intravenous administration of MSCs demonstrated efficacy (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.20–0.40); whereas intraperitoneal administration of MSCs did not have a statistically significant effect (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.02–1.89; Figure 2—figure supplement 4 ) and had high heterogeneity ( I 2 = 78%), suggesting a high degree of inter-study variability.

MSCs administered to mice were effective (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.15–0.36) however MSC administration to rats did not produce a statistically significant effect (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.18–1.21; Figure 2—figure supplement 6 ).
None of the experiments were considered low risk of bias across all six domains of methodological quality.
Visual inspection of a funnel plot analysis of all experiments suggested that publication bias exists ( Figure 4 ), which was confirmed by Egger regression (p=0.019).

Only two studies incorporated a majority of elements addressing construct validity (i.e. at least five of eight elements); there was no difference in effect size between these studies (OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.08–0.42) and those studies that incorporated fewer elements (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.17–0.44) ( Figure 2—figure supplement 11 ).

measurements.measures: the amount of previously unexplained variation in the data that was accounted for by litter effects
measurements.compared: analysis with litter effects vs. analysis without litter effects
measurements.verbatim: It is clear that litter-to-litter variation is important for a number of behavioural outcomes. It is also clear from Figure 3 A how one could obtain false positives with an inappropriate design and analysis. Suppose an experiment was conducted with only one VPA and one saline litter, with ten animals from each, and that there is no overall effect of VPA on a particular outcome. If the experimenter happened to select Litter A (saline) and Litter M (VPA) there would be a significant increase due to VPA, but if Litter D (saline) and Litter G (VPA) were selected, there would be a significant effect in the opposite direction! There are many combinations of a single saline and VPA litter that would lead to a significant difference between conditions. Having two or three litters per group instead of one will reduce the false positive rate, but it will still be much higher than 0.05 [4]. In addition, these apparent differences would not replicate with a properly designed follow-up experiment. 23522086.what_the_study_did: The study reviewed the literature on the valproic acid (VPA) model of autism in rodents to assess the quality of experimental design and statistical analysis, focusing on the handling of litter-to-litter variation.
23522086.what_it_found: A significant proportion of published studies in this model, and in preclinical research more broadly, suffer from poor experimental design and statistical analysis, particularly in accounting for litter effects, which can lead to inflated false positive rates and overstatement of treatment efficacy.

key_quotes.quote: Translation from in vivo animal models (typically rodent) has been poor, despite many years of research and effort.

Using actual body weight data from their experiment, Holson and Pearce showed that if three “treated” and three “control” litters are used, with two offspring per litter (total number of offspring = 12), then the false positive rate (Type I error) is 20% rather than the assumed 5% [4].

Holson and Pearce reported that only 30% of papers in the behavioural neurotoxicology literature correctly accounted for litter effects [4] and Zorrilla noted that 34% of papers in Developmental Psychobiology and 15% of papers in related journals correctly accounted for litter effects [5].
The main finding is that only 9% (3/34) of studies correctly identified the experimental unit and thus made valid inferences from the data.
The interpretation is that litter accounted for 61% of the previously unexplained variation in the data.

A two-group study with three litters per group and eight animals per litter (2 × 3 × 8 = 48 animals) will have only a 30% chance of detecting the effect, whereas a study with ten litters per group and one animal per litter (2 × 10 × 1 = 20 animals) will have almost 80% power and also use far fewer animals.
