12667944.what_the_study_did: The study compared preclinical cardiac electrophysiology data (in vitro and in vivo) with clinical QT interval prolongation and torsade de pointes (TdP) risk for 100 drugs.
12667944.what_it_found: A margin of 30-fold between effective therapeutic plasma concentration and hERG IC50 appears to be a demarcation between drugs associated with TdP and those that are not, though exceptions exist.

key_quotes.quote: A 30-fold margin between Cmax and hERG IC 50 may suffice for drugs currently undergoing clinical evaluation, but for future drug discovery programmes, pharmaceutical companies should consider increasing this margin, particularly for drugs aimed at non-debilitating diseases.

The dataset confirms the widely-held belief that most drugs associated with TdP in humans are also associated with hERG K 1 channel block at concentrations close to or superimposed upon the free plasma concentrations found in clinical use.
For drugs in Category 4 (‘isolated reports of TdP’), there was a wide range of margins, from 0.13-fold (sparfloxacin) to 35 700-fold (nifedipine).

Finally, for those drugs where there are no reports of TdP in clinical use (Category 5), the margins ranged from 23-fold to 3311-fold, with the exception of verapamil (1.7-fold) and ketoconazole (11fold).

Clearly we should focus on margins rather than absolute potency at the hERG K 1 channel: although all but one (grepafloxacin) of the drugs in Category 2 (‘withdrawn / suspended from the market due to TdP’) were more potent hERG /IKr blockers than any of the drugs in Category 5 (‘no reports of TdP’), the important differences between our 5 categories are to be found in the margin data (Fig. 2).
It is worthwhile discussing the limitations of our dataset before attempting to draw any conclusions from it.

35616311.what_the_study_did: This study reviews the evidence generated by systematic reviews of preclinical animal research to identify limitations and implications for preclinical research and medicine.
35616311.what_it_found: Systematic reviews have exposed significant shortcomings in the design, conduct, reporting, and translation of preclinical animal research, raising doubts about its robustness and clinical relevance.

key_quotes.quote: As more and more animal studies were scrutinised as part of the systematic review process, it gradually became apparent that much animal research was conducted to a low standard and was therefore unable to generate robust, reliable data.

In short, systematic reviews provided overwhelming evidence that animal studies suffer from poor experimental design and a lack of scientific rigour, raising doubts about the robustness of their findings and consequently, their clinical relevance.

Selective analysis and biased outcome reporting – the practice of reporting only the most positive outcomes and analyses from among the many performed and studied – was also revealed to be a problem in animal research.
This problem – which has come to be known as the reproducibility crisis – is due to poor experimental design and poor scientific conduct and is compounded by incomplete reporting.
They noted that shortcomings in almost every aspect of the scientific design, conduct and reporting of animal studies were contributing to an inability to translate into benefits for humans.
First, the inability of many, if not most animal models to replicate complex human diseases; and second, the problem of species differences.

36730203.what_the_study_did: The study developed and applied a computational framework called CAMO (Congruence Analysis for Model Organisms) to quantitatively evaluate the molecular congruence between animal models and human studies using transcriptomic data.
36730203.what_it_found: The CAMO framework can reconcile conflicting conclusions about model organism mimicry by providing quantitative measures of cross-species congruence, revealing condition-specific similarities and differences, and identifying specific pathways and gene modules that are concordant or discordant between species.

key_quotes.quote: Our CAMO result reconciles the two dichotomized and subjective conclusions of “greatly mimicking” or “poorly mimicking” by numerically quantifying the concordance and discordance of human–MM comparisons at genome-wide, pathway, or gene subnetwork module level.

MB and MI are overall more similar to the four human studies (HB, HI, HT, and HS) in a weaker congruence level (c-scores = 0.081 to 0.20; shaded pink, SI Appendix , Table S4 ) while MT, MS, MA, and ML have almost no genome-wide congruence, implying the concordance of cross-species transcriptomic response in inflammatory diseases is condition specific.

Intriguingly, although MI only shows moderate genome-wide cross-species c-score compared to intracohort c-score (median c-score = 0.15 for HI1 vs. MI vs. 0.43 for HI1 vs. HI2) in hsa04662, its cross-species c-scores in all four selected pathways are close to the human “ceilings” in SI Appendix , Fig. S4 B .
In contrast, MS has almost zero genome-wide and pathway-specific c-scores with all five human studies.
The complete c-score matrix and d-score matrix are shown in SI Appendix , Tables S8 and S9 , respectively.

We also propose intracohort and intercohort heterogeneity analyses in human to isolate experimental variabilities from true cross-species differences when the sample size in the human sepsis is sufficiently large and/or independent human studies are available for validation.

28731442.what_the_study_did: The study constructed computational cause-and-effect models of neuroinflammation for human and mouse using Biological Expression Language (BEL) based on published literature, and then compared these models at structural and functional levels to assess functional equivalence between the species.
28731442.what_it_found: The study found significant differences between human and mouse neuroinflammatory pathways at the molecular and cellular levels, with more similarities observed at the pathway level. These differences can explain failures in translating drug efficacy from mouse models to human clinical trials.

key_quotes.quote: Warren et al. re-confirmed essential differences between these two species at molecular level by showing that mouse models mimicked only 12% of the genes deregulated in human conditions [11].

At the molecular level, we found that 27% of cytokine interactions are similar in both species, 15% of interactions in mouse are found to be contradictory (opposite direction) to human, and 58% of interactions were found only in human or in other words, 58% of these human interactions are not proven with mouse experiments (Supplementary Table 4).

At the cellular level, based on the interactions among cell types (microglia and astrocytes), bioprocesses, and proteins, we found a relatively higher similarity between the two species. 62% of the interactions were similar between the species, 28% of interactions were found only in human, and 10% of interactions were found to be contradicting in human and mouse.

Excluding tissue specificity, expression patterns for 31% of genes in both species were the same, while 14% of genes from Fig. 3 were significantly expressed only in human and 19% of genes were expressed only in mouse.

The underlying molecular patterns which lead to a particular bioprocess differ between the two species. This finding implies that although the two species share some similarities at the cellular or pathway level, the pattern of molecular interactions that form, govern, and regulate those pathways is substantially different between mouse and human.

The fact that mimicking human disease pathology in mice using a chemical agent or a single gene is purely correlative and supports the notion that it is crucial to take the fundamental mechanistic differences between mouse and human into consideration when attempting to translate preclinical findings to clinical trials.

28335819.what_the_study_did: This study analyzed 33 Parkinson's disease microarray studies to investigate the impact of species, tissue, platform, and sample size on gene expression concordance.
28335819.what_it_found: The study found that concordance between microarray studies is generally low, but increases within human studies and studies focusing on specific tissues like the substantia nigra. Differences between human studies and animal models, and between different tissues, were more significant than those related to platform or sample size.

key_quotes.quote: The mean average pairwise correlation of differential gene expression signatures (i.e., the top 50 genes by absolute log fold change at a significance of p < 0.05, see Methods ) over all 33 Parkinson’s disease studies is 0.05 (Fig. 1 ), indicating little overall consensus as to which genes are differentially regulated in PD.
The average concordance of differential gene expression signatures across experiments increases from 0.05 over all PD studies to 0.15 in human in vivo studies.

In the subset of mouse studies, however, average concordance of differential gene expression decreases compared to the full dataset, at 0.03, and average concordance within the three rat studies is actually negative.

Limiting the studies under consideration to those of the basal ganglia (here including studies of the striatum and functionally also the substantia nigra), which is highly affected in PD, increases average gene-level concordance from 0.05 to 0.10, while further limiting the studies to just those of the substantia nigra yields a substantial increase to 0.30 (Fig. 1 ).

Over all data sets, 26% of the 43 genes called significant by our meta-analysis (Table 2 ) were included in the list of previously PD-associated genes. If the meta-analysis was limited to human studies, however, 36% of the 22 significant genes had previous evidence of association with PD (Fig. 6 ).

The results presented here confirm that the differences between human studies and model systems, and between tissues, are larger than those caused by other experimental factors such as microarray platform or sample size (Figs. 1 , 2 and 3 ).

25677548.what_the_study_did: The study compared blood biochemical profile responses to acute submaximal exercise between rats and humans under identical experimental conditions.
25677548.what_it_found: The study found that rats adequately mimic human responses to exercise in most basic blood biochemical profiles, with 26 out of 30 parameters showing similar directional changes and similar magnitudes of change after exercise.

key_quotes.quote: Our major finding is that the rat adequately mimics human responses to exercise in basic blood biochemical profile (i.e., iron status, lipid profile, glucose regulation, protein metabolism, liver and renal function).

The physiological resemblance of rat and human blood responses after acute exercise to exhaustion on the treadmill indicates that the wide use of rats in exercise physiology research is justified in the blood parameters determined in this study.
The changes in blood biochemical parameters in response to exercise have similar qualitative and quantitative characteristics for both rats and humans.
More specifically, 26/30 variables changed toward the same direction after exercise (qualitative agreement).
Likewise, the magnitude of these uniform changes was also very similar (7.9% in rats and 7.3% in humans; quantitative agreement).

Moreover, only two significant interactions were found between species and exercise (in testosterone and globulin), thus statistically verifying the similar pattern of blood responses following exercise in rats and humans.

36859342.what_the_study_did: The study investigated the accuracy of Investigator's Brochures (IBs) in predicting tolerable and pharmacologically active dose ranges for CNS drugs in humans by comparing preclinical animal data with clinical study results.
36859342.what_it_found: The study found that preclinical data can reasonably predict tolerable and pharmacologically active dose ranges in humans, with C max being the best predictor for tolerability and HED or AUC for pharmacological activity.

key_quotes.quote: The results demonstrate that tolerable and pharmacologically active dose ranges in clinical studies can be reasonably well predicted from preclinical data.
Tolerability was best predicted by C max and pharmacologically active ranges by HED or AUC.
We noted that despite recommendations by the EMA to base the starting dose on both NOAEL and MABEL, the starting dose is often solely based on the NOAEL.
In line with current literature [17], the internal validity of preclinical experiments was poor and preclinical in vivo CNS experiments are often performed without reporting PK results.
Thus, a considerable proportion of CNS active agents (28%) seem to have more prominent effects in humans than animals.

These results emphasize that in FIH studies with CNS active compounds, researchers should pay special attention to the psychiatric effects of new compounds, as these cannot be reliably predicted from animal experiments.
